text: Terrain, forecast rainfall, river-basin context, and historical-event ML evaluation
A usable resident interface backed by real spatial data, with research ML kept separate.
Select a neighbourhood and a 1, 2, or 5 km circle. Read terrain, forecast rainfall, and river-basin context in plain language.
React and Leaflet call FastAPI. A PostGIS-backed worker samples FABDEM, reads HydroSHEDS, and fetches Open-Meteo rainfall.
Compare real labels with Extra Trees and U-Net masks on held-out events. Classification models add event-level context.
A complete local demonstrator with transparent coverage states, reproducible deployment, visible model failures, and measured held-out performance.
Neighbourhood awareness only: no official warning, evacuation advice, depth estimate, or property flood probability.
Why local flood information is easy to misread
Raw surface elevation may treat buildings and trees as barriers. FloodLens uses bare-earth terrain and still reports its limits.
A mapped river near a point does not prove hydraulic connectivity to a street or property.
A simple number may be mistaken for a warning or probability. FloodLens labels its terrain score as a relative index.
Help residents understand the water around them while showing what the data cannot establish.

Terrain score: deterministic, local, and explainable
Moderate relative terrain susceptibility within the sampled circle.
It does not mean a 65% chance of flooding and it does not estimate water depth.
Terrain quality also reports valid-cell coverage and missing-data flags.

Research lab: two related ML tasks
The models study historical observed water. They do not produce the resident terrain score.

Does this 512 × 512 chip contain at least 5% labelled observed water?

Models: spatial gradient baseline and rainfall LSTM.

Output: one probability and a thresholded class.

Which pixels match the verified observed-water label?

Models: Extra Trees and a three-scale two-band U-Net.

Output: a water mask plus error overlay.
Training and evaluation stay in research/. The resident API never treats these predictions as warnings or property risk.
Validation selects checkpoints and thresholds; the test events remain unseen.
Six complete-rainfall events fit model weights.
USA and Sri Lanka select checkpoint and threshold.
Bolivia and Paraguay form the held-out evaluation.
Spain is excluded because its historical rainfall sequence is incomplete. Missing values are not imputed.
Event-held-out evaluation is harder and more honest than a random chip split.
Sentinel-1 VV/VH radar and 60 days of CHIRPS rain.
Spatial summaries or an LSTM estimate chip-level water.
Extra Trees and U-Net label each valid pixel.
VV/VH percentiles, distribution spread, cross-polarisation summaries, texture gradients, and transformed rainfall.
Two radar bands, augmented 128 × 128 crops, masked BCE plus Dice loss, and overlapping tiled inference.
The lab places both tasks beside the same held-out event so users can inspect agreement and failure.
Held-out results on Bolivia and Paraguay
Scores come from 81 chips across two unseen events and remain exploratory.
The LSTM reached PR-AUC 0.762, but threshold transfer reduced F1 to 0.293.
Classification and segmentation scores describe different tasks.
Historical Event Lab: comparison in the browser
Select an event and chip, change model, adjust opacity, and inspect run details.
Extra Trees and U-Net IoU/F1 appear beside chip-level classification.
The original LSTM remains visible because weak transfer is useful evidence.
The export points to the accepted baseline artifact and frozen segmentation run.
Failure analysis on a held-out satellite chip
Bolivia_129334 has full radar coverage, so the four panels can be compared without a confusing no-data swath.
The U-Net recovers most of the broad labelled water area. Remaining mistakes concentrate around narrow boundaries and small disconnected regions.
A higher F1 can still hide a bad model
The event-balanced LSTM v2 reached F1 0.603 by predicting every held-out chip as positive.
The apparent F1 improvement did not represent a useful decision rule.
It preserves positive and negative decisions, with PR-AUC 0.871 and ROC-AUC 0.909.
Model selection uses the confusion pattern and threshold-independent metrics, not F1 alone.

Final result: what a user receives
A completed assessment turns multiple technical data sources into a short, understandable neighbourhood summary.
Selected map point, exact coordinates when expanded, and the chosen 1 km, 2 km, or 5 km circle.
Relative terrain susceptibility, factor explanation, coverage ratio, and a clear statement that the score is not flood probability.
Provider, forecast window, total rainfall, intensity context, and an unavailable state if the provider cannot return data.
Containing basin, upstream context, nearest mapped river distance, and wording that prevents property-level interpretation.
Analysis ID, dataset status, import coverage, source versions, timing, technical JSON, and printable output.
The final screen starts with the information residents can act on, while detailed evidence stays available for review.

FloodLens successfully demonstrates how terrain, forecast rainfall, river-basin context, and historical-event ML analysis can be combined in one transparent project without presenting experimental predictions as public warnings.
Next scientific step: add more independent events and India-focused geography-held-out validation before considering resident-facing ML.
